title: I don't believe, but I'm curious
seoTitle: Curious About Christianity? What Christians Believe and Why
description: Curious about Christianity but not a believer? What Christians actually claim, the case for the resurrection and its limits, and how to look with no pressure.
summary: What Christians actually claim, the best reasons and the honest limits, and how to look for yourself. No tricks, no altar call.
askedAs: did Jesus rise from the dead
can I go to church if I don't believe
does the Bible call atheists fools
answer: You don't believe, or you're not sure there's anything to believe, and still the question won't leave you alone. It might be a friend whose faith you can't explain away, a funeral that left you wondering where the person went, or plain curiosity about a man people are still arguing over two thousand years later. You may also be wary of being sold something. That's fair. Nobody here will press you for a decision or ask you to sign anything. I came to faith from atheism, and I'd rather you look hard and walk away than believe something you never examined. If you want somewhere to start tonight, read the Gospel of Mark, the shortest of the four, as you'd read any ancient biography, and notice what surprises you.
happening:
Curiosity like this tends to stay private. You might find yourself reading about it late at night, or listening more closely than you let on when someone you respect talks about prayer, surprised the question matters to you at all. There's often wariness too. Some of the Christians you've met couldn't say why they believe, or seemed more interested in your vote than your questions. And taking this seriously can seem to mean switching off your mind, or losing the good opinion of people whose minds you admire.

People will explain the curiosity for you: a phase, a hard year, or, if they're Christians, God drawing you. None of that settles anything. A grieving or lonely person can still notice something real, and a question deserves to be judged on its merits, not on the mood you were in when you asked it. Christianity deserves the same fairness. You've probably met versions of it already: a list of rules for being good, a political identity with a flag on it, a comfort for people who can't face death, a demand to believe without evidence. Each of those exists, and Christians have given you reasons to distrust every one. None of them is what the faith says about itself at its center. Christianity doesn't present itself first as advice. It presents itself as news.

At the center are a claim about God and a claim about history. There is one God, who made everything that exists and is not part of it, who is personal rather than a force, and who is love; Christians confess this one God as Father, Son, and Holy Spirit. We were made to know him, and we have turned from him and wronged one another, and that wrong runs through every human heart, believers' included. Christians believe that in Jesus of Nazareth, a Jewish teacher executed by the Romans around AD 30, God himself came among us, fully human and fully God, and that his death on a cross was God's own act, God bearing in himself the cost of what we've done. They believe that on the third day he was raised from the dead, bodily, as an event in history, and that the whole faith stands or falls there. What follows is grace: forgiveness and new life given as a gift, received by trusting him, never earned by being good enough.

So the question in front of you is narrower than it may seem: whether a man executed under Pontius Pilate walked out of his grave, and what it would mean for you if he did.

scripture.intro: The New Testament expects skeptics. Its writers knew their central claim sounded impossible, and they wrote for people who would want reasons. These passages show how the first Christians met doubt: a scornful man invited to come and see, a writer who says he checked his sources, one of the oldest summaries of the faith with its witnesses named, and a speech to philosophers, some of whom mocked.

passages.text: Philip found Nathanael and told him, “We have found the One Moses wrote about in the Law, the One the prophets foretold—Jesus of Nazareth, the son of Joseph.” “Can anything good come from Nazareth?” Nathanael asked. “Come and see,” said Philip. When Jesus saw Nathanael approaching, He said of him, “Here is a true Israelite, in whom there is no deceit.”
passages.reading: Nathanael's first words about Jesus are a sneer at his hometown, Nazareth, a small village in Galilee. Later in this Gospel the Pharisees dismiss the whole region the same way: “no prophet comes out of Galilee” (John 7:52). Philip answers with three words: “Come and see.” When Jesus sees the skeptic coming, he commends him as a man “in whom there is no deceit,” as if an honest objection pleased him more than a polite pretense would have. What moves Nathanael is that Jesus knew where he had been before Philip called him, under a fig tree (John 1:48), and when he leaps to a sweeping confession, Jesus tells him he will see “greater things than these” (John 1:50). No one argues Nathanael into anything: he's invited to look, honored for his honesty, and told there is more to see, which is still the invitation.

passages.text: Many have undertaken to compose an account of the things that have been fulfilled among us, just as they were handed down to us by the initial eyewitnesses and servants of the word. Therefore, having carefully investigated everything from the beginning, it seemed good also to me to write an orderly account for you, most excellent Theophilus, so that you may know the certainty of the things you have been taught.
passages.reading: Luke's Gospel opens with a statement of method. Its writer says the material came from “the initial eyewitnesses” and that he had “carefully investigated everything from the beginning” before writing for Theophilus, who had already been taught about Jesus. The purpose is plain: so that Theophilus could “know the certainty” of what he'd heard. That isn't a demand to believe without reasons. It's an offer of reasons from someone who says he did the checking himself. His second volume to the same reader, the book of Acts, says the risen Jesus gave his followers “many convincing proofs that He was alive” (Acts 1:3). You're free to test whether the account holds.

passages.text: For what I received I passed on to you as of first importance: that Christ died for our sins according to the Scriptures, that He was buried, that He was raised on the third day according to the Scriptures, and that He appeared to Cephas and then to the Twelve. After that, He appeared to more than five hundred brothers at once, most of whom are still living, though some have fallen asleep. Then He appeared to James, then to all the apostles. And last of all He appeared to me also, as to one of untimely birth. ... And if Christ has not been raised, your faith is futile; you are still in your sins. ... If our hope in Christ is for this life alone, we are to be pitied more than all men.
passages.reading: This is one of the oldest summaries of the Christian faith we have. Paul wrote this letter in the mid-50s AD, roughly twenty years after the crucifixion, to a church where some were saying “there is no resurrection of the dead” (1 Corinthians 15:12). He reminds them of what he himself “received” and passed on, so the summary is older than the letter. It names witnesses: Cephas, that is, Peter (John 1:42), the Twelve, and more than five hundred at once, “most of whom are still living,” people who could still be asked. Last comes Paul, who had tried to destroy the church (Galatians 1:13). Then he says what follows if he is wrong: if Christ was not raised, “your faith is futile; you are still in your sins,” and Christians are “to be pitied more than all men.” The faith rests its whole weight on an event that could, in principle, be shown false, and it said so in writing within a generation.

passages.text: Then Paul stood up in the meeting of the Areopagus and said, “Men of Athens, I see that in every way you are very religious. For as I walked around and examined your objects of worship, I even found an altar with this inscription: TO AN UNKNOWN GOD. Therefore what you worship as something unknown, I now proclaim to you. ... Although God overlooked the ignorance of earlier times, He now commands all people everywhere to repent. For He has set a day when He will judge the world with justice by the Man He has appointed. He has given proof of this to everyone by raising Him from the dead.” When they heard about the resurrection of the dead, some began to mock him, but others said, “We want to hear you again on this topic.”
passages.reading: Paul is speaking before the council of the Areopagus in Athens, to an audience that included Epicurean and Stoic philosophers (Acts 17:18), people who shared neither his Scriptures nor his God. He begins with what they already have, an altar in their city and a line from their own poets (Acts 17:28), and then states the claim without softening it: God now commands everyone everywhere to repent, he has set a day of judgment, and he has given public proof of it by raising Jesus from the dead. Some mocked; resurrection sounded no more sensible in Athens than it does to many people now. Others said, “We want to hear you again on this topic.” Then Paul left the meeting, and some followed him and believed (Acts 17:33-34). If you're in that middle group, unconvinced and unfinished, you're standing where some of the first hearers stood, and Acts records them without scorn.

whyHard:
It's easy to assume that people once believed this because they didn't know any better, and that we stopped because we learned more. The first audiences don't fit that story. They knew the dead stay dead. When the women came back from the tomb, their report struck the apostles as “nonsense” (Luke 24:11), and Paul wrote that a crucified Messiah was “a stumbling block to Jews and foolishness to Gentiles” (1 Corinthians 1:23). What the modern world added was a sharper argument. In an essay on miracles published in 1748, the Scottish philosopher David Hume argued that a wise person proportions belief to the evidence. Our experience that nature keeps its regular course is as uniform as experience gets, he said, while testimony often errs, so a report of a miracle deserves belief only if its being false would be more miraculous than the miracle itself, and he judged that no such report had ever met that bar. That is the objection at full strength, and much of it is right. Witnesses get things wrong, and plenty of miracle stories fall apart once someone checks.

But the weighing depends on a question settled before any report arrives. If there is no God, no report of a resurrection could ever be believable, and any natural explanation, however strained, should win. If there is a God who made the world, a resurrection isn't absurd; it becomes a question of whether he did it. So the evidence for Easter can't be weighed in a sealed room. It comes paired with the question of God, and all of us, believers and skeptics alike, bring some answer to that question before we've read a word of the evidence. That's the honest limit of the Christian case: it can show that belief is reasonable, but it can't argue anyone out of a conclusion reached before the argument began. Neither can Hume's.

Meanwhile the word faith changed its meaning. Lesslie Newbigin, a British missionary who spent decades in India and then looked at his own culture with a missionary's eyes, argued in *Foolishness to the Greeks* (1986) that the modern West had sorted life into a public world of facts, which every reasonable person must accept, and a private world of values, which each of us chooses, and that religion had been filed with the values. A private preference can't be wrong, which means it can't be right either. Christians helped make it so. We told people to *just believe*, treated hard questions as disloyalty, sold the faith as a way to feel better or a badge for our side, and sometimes used the fear of hell to close a sale. I'm a pastor, and that charge reaches me. If that's the Christianity you've refused, you were right to refuse it.

Underneath all of it sits a suspicion that's harder to put into words: that people believe because they need to. Sigmund Freud gave it its best-known form in *The Future of an Illusion* (1927). Belief in God, he argued, grows out of the helplessness we felt as children, and it promises exactly what a frightened child would wish for: a father strong enough to protect us, a moral order that finally sets things right, and a life that doesn't end at death. When a belief matches our wishes that closely, he reasoned, we should suspect the wish of writing it. I was raised without a father, and I'm a pastor who calls God Father, so I can't wave that charge away. Some faith is exactly what Freud described. But Freud himself granted that an illusion, in his sense, isn't necessarily false, though he plainly thought this one was. A longing can explain why someone wants a thing without settling whether the thing is there; thirst doesn't prove there's water, and it doesn't prove there isn't. The suspicion also cuts both ways. There are strong reasons to want no God at all, no one to answer to and no claim on how I live, and those wishes prove nothing either. Freud's method can tell you a good deal about the believer and the skeptic, and nothing about God.

So the question was never whether you're smart enough to believe. It's whether any of us, you and I alike, can look at it without deciding first.

thisWeek.intro: Nothing here needs deciding by Sunday, and none of it asks you to pretend. These are ways to look honestly, at your own pace. Start with the first; the others can wait until you want them.

steps.title: Read one Gospel, start to finish
steps.body: Read [the Gospel of Mark](/study/bible/mark/1) straight through, in an evening or two. Leave the commentaries and summaries for later, this page included. Notice what Jesus says and does, what the people around him get wrong, and what strikes you as strange or hard, and write your questions in the margin as they come. You're reading the book as it is, before anyone has explained it to you.

steps.title: Name your real objection
steps.body: Write down, in one sentence, what most keeps you from believing: suffering, science, the church's record, the harder passages in the Bible, or simply that the dead stay dead. Then write a second sentence: *What would count as good evidence for me, and what would count against?* It's a question believers ought to ask themselves too. It keeps you honest in both directions and gives any conversation somewhere real to go.

steps.title: Talk with a Christian who can take questions
steps.body: Look for someone who listens well and can say *I don't know* without flinching, whether a thoughtful friend or a pastor. Ask plainly: *I'm not a believer, but I'm curious. Can I ask you hard questions without being recruited?* A good one will say yes and mean it, and won't hurry you toward an answer. If someone meets your questions with pressure or flattery, thank them and find someone else; their nerves aren't evidence either way.

steps.title: Visit a church as an observer
steps.body: You're allowed to come and watch. Choose a church, sit near the back, and see what they actually say and do. You don't have to sing, give money, fill out a card, or explain yourself. If bread and wine or juice are passed, you can let them go by; many churches ask that only those who believe take them. Notice whether the sermon opens a passage of the Bible or only tells you how to feel, and if anyone pressures you, leave.

steps.title: Weigh the best case against the best objection
steps.body: Give both sides their strongest voice. [Can a Reasonable Person Believe in Miracles?](/writing/apologetics-can-a-reasonable-person-believe-in-miracles) states Hume's argument at full strength before answering it, and [Did the Gospels Get Jesus Right?](/resources/context/did-the-gospels-get-jesus-right) takes on the idea that the stories drifted into legend. Then read the best skeptical scholars on the same questions, in their own words, and notice where each side has to strain to make its case.

moreHelp.body:
Curiosity about God usually calls for reading, honest conversation, and time rather than a professional. Sometimes, though, the question arrives tangled with something heavier. If it came with a death or a long stretch of despair, and the heaviness has reached your sleep, appetite, or work, see a doctor or a licensed counselor alongside your reading. If a fear of hell from childhood still brings panic, a counselor can help you separate the fear from the question. If the questions have turned into not wanting to be alive, call or text 988 now.

Seekers can also be taken advantage of. If a group you're exploring demands secrecy, pressures you for money, pushes you away from family and friends, or treats questions as betrayal, step back and talk with someone outside it. If someone at home hurts or threatens you, including over what you believe, in either direction, that is abuse. If you're in danger, call 911; if you're afraid of someone at home, the help lines at the end of this page can help you plan for safety.

To find a counselor, ask your doctor for a referral, check your insurer's directory, or ask a pastor which counselors nearby they trust. Make sure they're licensed in your state, and say that you want someone who won't push you toward faith or away from it.
signs: You've had thoughts of not wanting to be alive. Call or text 988 now, or 911 if you're in danger.
A heaviness that came with the questions has lasted two weeks or more and reached your sleep, appetite, or work.
A fear of hell or of God's anger brings panic or keeps you awake, and nothing settles it for long.
A religious group demands secrecy, pressures you for money, or pulls you away from family and friends.
You're afraid of someone at home, or they hurt or threaten you, including over what you believe. If you're in danger, call 911.
moreHelp.firstCall: Keep it simple: *I've been looking into questions about God, and it's stirring up more than I expected. I'm not a believer, and I want a counselor who won't push me either way.* Say what has changed in your sleep, mood, or work, and for how long. If you'd rather call a church first, try: *I'm not a Christian, but I'm curious. Would someone meet with me and take hard questions, knowing I may never join?* A good pastor will say yes.
moreHelp.cost: Talking with a pastor costs nothing, and [the Study Bible](/study/bible) on this site is free to read. Counseling fees vary, so ask about sliding-scale fees based on income, look for a community mental health center or a university training clinic, and check whether your employer offers an employee assistance program, which often includes a few free sessions.

helping.body:
If someone has told you they don't believe but they're curious, they've trusted you with something, and your first job is to keep it safe for them to keep asking. Ask what got them curious, and listen longer than you want to. Resist the urge to close the deal; people can tell when they've become a project, and it ends the conversation. The first letter of Peter tells Christians to be ready to give “the reason for the hope that is in you” and, in the same breath, to “respond with gentleness and respect” (1 Peter 3:15). We tend to remember the first half.

Name the church's failures before they have to, and don't claim more certainty than you have. Let the friendship stand whether or not they ever believe. If you're married to someone who doesn't share your faith, live it in front of them more than you argue it. If you're a pastor, preach as though a skeptic is in the room, because one may be. Pastors carry a particular temptation to treat a curious person as a decision to be won, and I'm not exempt.
say: I'm glad you told me. What got you curious?
That's a fair objection. Let's look at it honestly.
I don't have a good answer to that yet. Can I come back to you?
Want to read Mark with me? No strings attached.
Whatever you decide, nothing changes between us.
dontSay: You just have to have faith.
So when are you going to decide?
helping.next: Offer one concrete thing: read Mark together over a couple of weeks, or go with them to a service and talk afterward about what they saw. If they want to go further alone, point them to the plan or a study further down this page. When a question is beyond you, bring in a pastor, with their permission. [How to Welcome a Skeptic to Your Table](/how-tos/dm-how-to-welcome-a-skeptic-to-your-table) is worth reading first. Then pray for them quietly, and leave the outcome with God.

prayer:
God, if you are there, I don't know that you are. I'm not ready to pretend, and I don't want to be fooled, by anyone else or by myself.

If you're real, I would rather know than be comfortable. Show me what is true, even if it costs me something. Nathanael was told to come and see, and I'm willing to look. Thomas wanted to see the wounds, and so do I. If my reasons for not believing are good ones, keep me honest about them. If some of them are fear, or pride, or an old hurt wearing the clothes of an argument, let me see that too.

I won't promise you anything tonight. A father once cried out to Jesus that he believed and needed help with his unbelief; I can't say the first part yet. But if you are there, I'm listening, and I'm asking you not to stay silent.

faq.q: Is there any real evidence that Jesus existed?
faq.a: Yes. Even scholars who reject the Christian faith generally accept that Jesus lived and was crucified; Bart Ehrman, a New Testament scholar who is not a believer, defended his existence against those who deny it in *Did Jesus Exist?* (2012). Paul's letters, written within a generation of the crucifixion, mention people who knew Jesus, including his brother (Galatians 1:19). The Roman historian Tacitus, writing early in the second century, says Christ was executed under Pontius Pilate, and the Jewish historian Josephus mentions Jesus too, though most scholars think the longer of his two passages was expanded by later Christian copyists. Beyond the bare facts of his life and death, those outside sources say little. Who he was is the real question, and the Gospels are where you'll have to weigh it.

faq.q: Isn't faith just believing without evidence?
faq.a: In the New Testament, faith means trust, the kind you place in a person once you have reason to, the way you trust a surgeon with a good record or marry someone you've come to know. Trust always reaches a little past what you can verify, so faith is never proof, but it's meant to rest on reasons rather than replace them. Luke's Gospel was written so a reader could “know the certainty” of what he'd been taught (Luke 1:4). When Thomas asked for evidence, Jesus showed him his hands (John 20:27). He did add, “blessed are those who have not seen and yet have believed” (John 20:29), but the next lines say what later readers are given in place of sight: an account “written so that you may believe” (John 20:31), testimony to weigh. A church that treats wanting reasons as a lack of faith is asking for something its own Scriptures don't.

faq.q: Doesn't the Bible call atheists fools?
faq.a: Psalm 14, which bears David's name, opens with that line: “The fool says in his heart, ‘There is no God.’” Christians have sometimes used it as a put-down, but the psalm describes people who live as if no one will ever hold them to account, not philosophers weighing arguments: “They devour my people like bread” (Psalm 14:4). Its Hebrew word for fool, nabal, is also the name of a rich man in 1 Samuel who was “harsh and evil in his dealings” and whose own wife said, “His name means Fool” (1 Samuel 25:3, 25). When Paul quotes the psalm's next lines, he aims them at everyone, the religious included: “Are we any better? Not at all” (Romans 3:9). In his hands the line stops being something to throw at unbelievers and becomes a mirror for everyone, the religious reader included.

faq.q: If God is good, why is there so much suffering?
faq.a: Many people, believers among them, find this the strongest objection to faith, and it deserves that weight. Christians don't have a tidy answer, and the Bible doesn't pretend to; it keeps Job's protest and whole psalms of complaint in its pages. What Christianity offers first is not an explanation that makes suffering make sense but a God who entered it: at the center of the faith is the cross, where Jesus cried out the opening line of Psalm 22, a lament, “My God, My God, why have You forsaken Me?” (Mark 15:34). That doesn't close the question, but it changes who stands inside it with you. [Why would God let this happen?](/help/suffering) goes further.

faq.q: Did Jesus really rise from the dead?
faq.a: No one can prove it the way you prove a theorem, and no honest Christian should claim to. What Christians offer is a case. Jesus's execution under Pontius Pilate is recorded by the Roman historian Tacitus, not only by Christians. In a letter written about twenty years later, Paul passed on an older summary naming those he says saw Jesus alive, among them Peter, more than five hundred at once, and Paul himself, who had persecuted the church (1 Corinthians 15:3-9). Jews who hoped for resurrection expected it at the last day, as Martha tells Jesus after her brother's death (John 11:24), yet his followers proclaimed that it had already happened to one man, in the city where he had been executed (Acts 2:32). The limits are real: the witnesses all became believers, the accounts differ in details, and whether a resurrection seems possible depends on whether you think there's a God who could do it. The case can make belief reasonable. It can't make it unavoidable.

slots.note: The page says once, in the answer, that James came to faith from atheism, with no story. If he chooses, he could add in his own words what kept him from belief and what moved him, written for a reader standing where he once stood, as a short paragraph before the closing verdict of Why this is so hard. The page stands without it. Several library pieces carry first-person accounts of his atheist years that this page does not repeat and that no one has confirmed with him. Among those this page links: the plan Eight Weeks of Reading Like an Adult (its introduction and week one), Test the Case (the openings and answers of several cases, including a line about unbelievers he has known), the hero of The Skeptic's Track, the Resurrection study guide (which says he came to faith by being unable to explain the evidence away), and the essay Did the Resurrection Actually Happen?. Unlinked: Is Faith Just Wishful Thinking?, What the New Atheists Got Right, Are Miracles Believable?, and How Does an Atheist Become a Christian, and a Pastor?. Anything added here should come from James himself, and he may want those pieces checked against his own account.

The answer gives James a stance in his own voice: that he would rather a reader look hard and walk away than believe something never examined. It follows the Writing Toward the Skeptic standard, but it is his conviction to confirm or reword.

The Freud paragraph states only that James was raised without a father and is a pastor who calls God Father, so he cannot wave away Freud's charge that belief grows from a longing for a protecting father; the answer to Freud rests on Freud's own point that an illusion is not necessarily false, not on anyone's motives. Whether that charge played any part in his own unbelief or his coming to faith is his to say, in his own words, beside that paragraph; the page stands without it. The essay Is Faith Just Wishful Thinking? tells a version of that story in his voice that has not been confirmed with him.

reviewed.notes: Second-pass edit, 2026-10-01, done from the top. Validator clean (node scripts/validate-needs.mjs curious) and the CarePage render test passes. Truth: the outside sources could not be reopened here (the source sites are blocked and search was unavailable), so each claim was kept only where it is ordinary, well-established knowledge, stated no more strongly than that; re-open every source before release. Hume (1748) is now stated as he argued it (belief proportioned to evidence; testimony believed only if its falsehood would be more miraculous than the event; his judgment that no report had met that bar), not as the claim that no report could ever outweigh experience, and the reply no longer says his argument smuggles in an assumption; it says the weighing depends on the question of God, for both sides. Freud, The Future of an Illusion (1927), is now stated at full strength before any answer (childhood helplessness; the wished-for protecting father, moral order, and life after death; suspect the wish), and answered from his own point that an illusion is not necessarily false, with the motive argument turned both ways and disowned as proof against anyone. Kept as certain: Newbigin, Foolishness to the Greeks (1986), on public facts and private values; Tacitus, Annals 15.44; Josephus, with the expansion of his longer passage now attributed to most scholars; Ehrman, Did Jesus Exist? (2012), now named; nabal in Psalm 14:1 and 1 Samuel 25:25; the crucifixion around AD 30 under Pilate.
